properties.name: Dead Sea
properties.tooltip:
Dead Sea
Southeastern frontier of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Its western shore lay within the royal domain of Jerusalem; the eastern shore belonged to the Lordship of Oultrejordain, whose castles of Kerak and Montreal overlooked it from the plateau. Crusader salt works operated on the western shore, and the balsam and bitumen of its shores were celebrated in medieval chronicles. In 1177 King Baldwin IV's army crossed near its northern end on the way to Montgisard. Raynald of Châtillon built the galleys of his 1183 Red Sea raid at Kerak on this shore and hauled them overland across Oultrejordain.

properties.name: Sea of Galilee
properties.tooltip:
Sea of Galilee (Lake Tiberias)
The freshwater heart of the Principality of Galilee. Tiberias, the principality's capital, sat on its western shore and controlled the Jordan crossings. Crusader-era pilgrim accounts linger on the lake's gospel associations — the Mount of the Beatitudes, Capernaum, and the stone Galilee fishing boats drawn up on its beaches. In July 1187 Count Raymond III of Tripoli's wife was besieged in Tiberias's citadel; the Frankish army's march to relieve her across the parched hills led directly to the catastrophe at the Horns of Hattin, which ended the first Kingdom of Jerusalem.

properties.name: Lake Semechonitis (Huleh)
properties.tooltip:
Lake Semechonitis (Lake Huleh)
A shallow marshy lake fed by the headwaters of the Jordan, lying within the Lordship of Toron. Crusader sources know it as Semechonitis, the classical Greek name. Its reed-choked shore offered poor grazing but rich waterfowl, and the high-road from Damascus to Acre skirted its northern bank. The lake was drained in the 1950s; only the preserved Huleh Nature Reserve now hints at the landscape the Franks knew.

properties.name: Red Sea (Gulf of Aqaba)
properties.tooltip:
Red Sea (Gulf of Aqaba)
Southern limit of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Control of the gulf's head was key to taxing the Egypt–Arabia pilgrim and caravan traffic; the Crusader castle of Île de Graye on Pharaoh's Island was built here c. 1116 for that purpose. In 1182–83 Raynald of Châtillon launched his infamous raid on the Hejaz coast from here, after dragging galleys in sections overland from Kerak — briefly bringing Frankish ships within sight of Mecca's port of Rabigh. Saladin's fleet annihilated the expedition in 1183.
